Memory, music, inheritance · 2017

CocoWhen Memory Becomes a Living Conversation

Marina’s Dreams reviews Pixar’s Coco, exploring how music, family memory, and Mexican visual traditions turn inheritance into a living conversation.

By MarinaOctober 17, 20263 min readSpoiler-light review

In this review

A World Built from Memory and MusicThe Cost of Turning Feeling into MeaningSources & references
Film
Coco
Director
Lee Unkrich
Year
2017

Coco begins with a deceptively simple conflict: Miguel loves music, while his family has made music the one thing a Rivera must not touch. What gives the film its lift is the way this argument is staged not as a battle between freedom and repression, but as a clash between different forms of care. Miguel’s desire is urgent and personal; the family’s rules are shaped by a story they believe protects them. The result is a coming-of-age film alert to how inheritance can feel both like shelter and a locked door.

A World Built from Memory and Music

The film’s most distinctive achievement is visual. Santa Cecilia feels sun-washed, handmade, and inhabited, while the Land of the Dead rises in extravagant layers, a city built from memory and continuously expanding history. Marigold petals form a glowing passage between worlds, and family altars turn remembrance into something tactile: photographs, food, flowers, objects placed with intention. These details do more than decorate the fantasy. They give the film a precise emotional geography, where the past is not behind the living but arranged beside them, waiting to be tended.

Sound carries that geography forward. Mexican musical traditions, original songs, and Michael Giacchino’s score make music feel less like a prize Miguel wants to win than a language through which people recognize one another. The voice performances are similarly well judged. Anthony Gonzalez gives Miguel a clear, restless sincerity, while Gael García Bernal lets Héctor’s jokes fray at the edges. Even the broad comic figures have expressive rhythms. Coco understands that a song can hold a family argument, a public performance, and a private plea at once.

I am especially drawn to the film’s treatment of memory. It avoids presenting remembrance as a grand monument; instead, it depends on ordinary acts of attention. A name spoken, a picture displayed, a tune carried forward—these gestures make identity feel communal rather than owned. The film’s Mexico is lovingly constructed, and its research is visible in the textures of streets, workshops, cemeteries, and celebrations. That care matters because the story asks us to enter a culture through its particular practices, not through a vague idea of exotic color.

The Cost of Turning Feeling into Meaning

Still, Coco sometimes presses its emotional buttons with the confidence of a machine that knows exactly when to turn the dial. The plot’s revelations arrive in a familiar sequence, and the message about family and artistic freedom can sound tidier than the complicated choices that lead there. Its crowded world also leaves some characters more emblematic than fully developed. Yet the polish is not empty. The film’s sentimentality is earned most convincingly when it stays with small gestures rather than announcing what they mean.

What remains with me is the film’s refusal to make belonging and self-expression enemies forever. Miguel does not simply escape tradition, and the family does not remain a wall around him. Their relationship has to be re-heard, as though an old melody might contain notes no one noticed before. That idea gives Coco its quiet force beneath the color and spectacle. It is a generous animated film, but also a thoughtful one: it treats the past as a living conversation, and music as the room where that conversation can begin.
